name: Tobagonian / TobC, in 'The creoles of Trinidad and Tobago'

catalog_quote: Solomon (1993: 34) identifies pitch as the critical prosodic feature rather than stress although he admits it is difficult to abstract pitch from tone. [...] The features of pitch and stress are confounded between English and Trinidadian speakers, the former hearing Trinidad pitch as stress. [...] The result is that disyllable words are most often either high-low or low-high, the latter being the more common and older pattern; in trisyllable words it is common to find a low-low-high or high-high-low pattern. [...] All this can often result in a change of the characteristic English pattern such that unstressed syllables in that variety often come to carry high pitch in Trinidadian. [...] (Capitals indicate stress, apostrophes denote pitch) COCKroa’ch, MAChine; TRInida’d; CARpe’nte’r. [...] James (2003) analyses the role of tone in the organisation of grammatical morphemes in a number of the subsystems of TobC. Among his findings about tone are that: a) In TobC tone is morphemic in the case of the homophones kyã ‘can’ vs. kyã ‘can’t’); b) In TobC tone distinguishes emphatic from non-emphatic meanings in the homophones dèm vs. dém; c) In TobC tone typically combines with rhyme length to distinguish the members of emphatic-nonemphatic pairs—high tone with long-vowel and vowel-consonant sequences, and low tone with single vowels (e.g., shíí vs. shì and dém vs dè)

new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional word-stress rule is given for Tobagonian. The primary describers treat word prosody in Trinidad & Tobago creoles as pitch-based rather than stress-based: each word carries a lexically specific pitch pattern (disyllables high-low or, more commonly, low-high; trisyllables low-low-high or high-high-low), English lexical stress positions are largely retained but syllables unstressed in English often carry high pitch, and (editor's synopsis from the same authors' checklist) stress is 'not infrequently' shifted from the first to a later syllable in TobC (indiˈcate, holiˈday); rhythm is syllable-timed with few reduced vowels. For the Tobagonian basilect specifically, H vs L tone (with rhyme length) is reported to be morphemic on grammatical morphemes (kyã 'can' vs 'can't', dèm vs dém; James 2003), and stressed/unstressed and high-/low-toned are used as interchangeable labels for function-word pairs. Hence coded lexical (word-specific prominence, no edge/weight rule), with pitch accent/residual-tone as the live alternative coding.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Tobagonian (the synopsis remark on secondary stress concerns American English).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift to a later syllable 'not infrequently' (indiˈcate, holiˈday; Schneider 2004:1087-8 for T&TC and TobC); Trinidadian salad /sæˈlaːd/ with final stress vs TobC 'two short vowels' (2004:516); Table 3 TobC forms with marked stressed syllable incl. war.TA 'water', DA.ddy, HA.ppy, KAN.fident (2004:519); compounds take H on the last syllable of the last word and L on the preceding word (James & Youssef 2004:457); homophones distinguished by pitch 'without necessarily changing the stress' (TE.la HL 'tailor' vs te.LA LH 'Taylor', 2004 vol.2:456).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level pitch/stress patterns on citation words (Solomon-derived description is explicitly of Trinidadian and the shared Trinidad-Tobago mesolect; the basilectal Tobagonian material concerns tone on grammatical morphemes and phrase-final intonation). Yakpo 2021 (second-hand) classes Tobagonian as 'contrastive word stress; no tone in the majority lexicon; residual tone' and notes the tonal analysis lacks acoustic verification.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted passage is from a chapter covering both Trinidadian (trin1276) and Tobagonian (toba1282); its word-prosody statement (pitch not stress; H-L / L-H disyllables) is taken over from Solomon 1993, a grammar of Trinidadian, and the authors say Trinidad and Tobago can be treated together only at the acrolectal/mesolectal levels while the Tobagonian basilect (TobC) must be considered separately. The TobC-specific content is (i) morphemic H/L tone with rhyme length on grammatical morphemes (James 2003), (ii) the compilers synopsis entries for TobC (stress shift to later syllables not infrequent; syllable-timed; tone distinctions characteristic; no high-rising terminals). The same passage underlies the existing trin1276 catalog entry (coded lexical). Provenance caveat: the vol. 1 text read is an on-disk file the compilers downloaded from vdoc.pub (a copy whose provenance we do not cite); I did not re-download it; wording of the key sentence opening is independently confirmed by a Google Books snippet of the 2008 reprint (p.334), and the vol. 2 passages come from a university-library-hosted PDF.
